text: Hey, everybody. Hope you're doing well. I wanted to make a video and talk a little bit about Psalm 82. My favorite psalm.
Now, this is a controversial psalm. There are people who read it very differently from the way I read it.
There are people who think it says nothing about other gods. There are other people who agree with me that it does.
But I want to read it from the NRSV, the New Revised Standard Version. I wanna talk about some of the translation issues there, some of the ways other people read it,
and then I wanna explain what I think the psalm is doing. And then I wanna talk about how it is being quoted by Jesus in John chapter 10,
and why I suggest that Jesus' reading of the psalm in John is different from how it was originally understood and what it was likely originally intended to accomplish.
So, let's get into the psalm. This is from the New Revised Standard Version: God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment:
“How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? Give justice to the weak and the orphan; maintain the right of the lowly and the destitute.
Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked.” They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk around in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken.
I say, “You are gods, children of the Most High, all of you;
nevertheless, you shall die like mortals, and fall like any prince.” Rise up, O God, judge the earth; for all the nations belong to you!
Now, I wanna divide this up into five portions: the introduction; verses 2, 3, and 4; verse 5; verses 6 and 7; and then finally verse 8.
Now, the introduction is pretty simple: God has taken his place in the divine council. In the midst of the gods he holds judgment.
We have the word אלהים occurring in there twice and then the word אל once.
Uh, אלהים is a generic term for "deity," or "deities," or it can be used adjectively as "divine."
It does not mean "judges." Um, it has never meant "judges" in the Hebrew Bible.
This is part of what people have called the Elohistic Psalter. And this is a reference to a chunk of the psalms that, rather than predominantly referring to the God of Israel as יהוה,
predominantly refers to the God of Israel as אלהים, and יהוה is more rare.
Now, there are different theories about why this is, what it is trying to accomplish, did someone go through and change a bunch of occurrences of יהוה to אלהים,
or did these people compose these psalms originally in reference to אלהים?
That's not critical to what I'm talking about, but just so you know, the first occurrence of אלהים is universally recognized as singular and as a reference to יהוה,
So יהוה takes his stand בעדת־אל, which is "in the council of El."
And this is—the אל there is usually interpreted adjectively, so "the divine council,"
but this is directly cognate with a phrase from the Ugaritic literature that refers to the council of El, with El functioning as the name of the patriarchal high deity.
And that could be what's going on here. It also could be a corruption of an originally plural עדת־אלים.
That may be what is—was in the source text of the Septuagint translator, cuz they render θεοι, the plural,
instead of the singular אל, θεος. So that is really the only textual—piece of textual instability that we find in Psalm 82 For the most part, it's pretty secure.
So some folks used to argue that the first אלהים was originally יהוה—probably just אלהים.
But we have—but a reference to יהוה. So, they take their stand in the council of אל
amidst the gods, so the second occurrence of אלהים is plural—amidst the gods—ישׁפט, he judges, or holds judgment.
So this introduces a pretty stereotypical divine council court scene.
The divine council is God, who sits on their throne and who is sovereign over this council made up of a bunch of other deities.
Now here we have God rising to judge in some way, so in addition to just the notion of a council,
we also have the notion of judgment taking place, this is a court now, rather than just council chambers.
And then we've got the second segment, verses 2, 3, and 4. Now, here we're moving away from the divine council type scene.
We have עד־מתי, how long, and then we have serial imperatives, a series of imperatives that demand someone meet
kind of a expectation regarding behavior. Now this actually is most closely related to the lament or the complaint psalm,
which is a pattern that we find where the psalmist is complaining to God, and says עד־מתי, how long
are you going to let this happen, are you going to do this, and then a series of imperatives— rise up, y'know, do justice, save us, whatever. There are a bunch of different ways that this manifests.
However, here it's not singular, it's not in reference to God, it's in the plural,
and it seems to be the content of the case that יהוה is making within the divine council.
And יהוה seems to be accusing the gods of the divine council—how long will you judge unjustly, show partiality to the wicked?
And then the serial imperatives—give justice to the weak and the orphan; maintain the right of the lowly and the destitute.
Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked. Another part of the lament or the complaint psalm
is the next segment, verse 5, where usually what the psalmist will do is describe the lamentable state of affairs
This is how bad it has gotten. And here, however, the referent seems to shift, because it's no longer second person plural,
it now shifts to third person plurals. They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk around in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken.
And so some folks understand this to be a reference to the weak and the needy. Rescue the weak and the needy.
Look at 'em. They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk around in darkness. Alternatively, within the divine council court scene framework, this may be a reference to the reader,
or to whoever is reigning, or sitting in judgment over the divine council. Another accusation, they—the gods—have neither nor understanding, they walk around in darkness;
all the foundations of the earth are shaken.
So then verses 6 and 7—we depart from the complaint motif and we're back in the divine council and we get what seem to be
the verdict and a sentence. The verdict is—basically, they're guilty. I say you are gods, children of the Most High, all of you;

nevertheless, you shall die like mortals, and fall like any prince. Now, this is one of the things that has become a proof text for those who would suggest that this is not a reference to gods but to mortals. God's don't die,
and it says you shall die like mortals. Well, gods do die. That's something we find in a number of extra-biblical texts from around this time and around this place.
So, their consignment to mortality is not a deal-breaker. So this seems to be, I would suggest, a verdict and a sentence.
And then the last verse of the psalm, Rise up, O God, judge the earth; for all the nations belong to you.
I wanna pause here, and I wanna drill down a little bit in this verse.
קומה אלהים, rise up, O God. שׁפטה הארץ, judge the earth, and then what the NRSV has rendered "all the nations belong to you,"
I would suggest is better rendered "for you shall inherit all nations," cuz the root there is נחל,
it's תנחל, "you will inherit," or "you shall take possession of."
Now here's why I think this is significant: קומה אלהים only occurs in one other place in all the Hebrew Bible,

and that is in Psalm 74, and that is another complaint psalm. And in that psalm, they're complaining about the destruction of the temple. Foreigners have come in, have destroyed the temple, are wreaking havoc.

And this is complaining about the exile, most likely. Some folks think it is dated to the eighth century and it's talking about the destruction of the cult sites in the northern kingdom, when the Assyrian empire came in,
but most likely this is talking about the exile. Fits with the Psalms of Asaph and their situation within the exile.
Rise up, O God, it says in Psalm 74, ריבה ריבך, plead your case.
Now this is why I think this is interesting, this connection. Cuz Psalm 74, this complaint psalm, is part of a,
kind of, two cycles—narrative cycles—that folks like Zenger and Hossfeld have pointed out that end in Psalm 82 or 83.
But the case that the psalmist is calling on God to rise up and plead I would argue is precisely what is happening in Psalm 82.
Rise up, O God, plead your case. Psalm 82 starts with God taking their stand—נצב—taking their place,
and pleading their case. Holding judgment among the gods.
So, if Psalm 74 is what inspires Psalm 82, and Psalm 82 is the response and resolution to Psalm 74,
then it must obviously follow chronologically. Psalm 74 talking about the nations coming in and destroying God's home and carrying off the exiles.
Psalm 82 must be responding to that as well. And this is what I suggest is going on here in Psalm 82,
that we've got a combination of two different literary genres. We've got the divine council type-scene, and then we've got a psalm of complaint, and they're being merged together.
But rather than the psalm of complaint coming from the psalmist and being directed at יהוה,
we take the psalm of complaint and we put it into the mouth of יהוה, and we direct it at the gods of the nations,

and accuse the gods of the nations of negligence regarding their duties as members of the divine council to maintain the cosmic order. So what have they done wrong? They have allowed a foreign nation to invade Israel,
to destroy God's house, and then to carry off captives into exile. So in so doing, they have shaken the foundations of the earth.
They have judged unjustly, they have shown partiality to the wicked, they have denied the weak and the orphan their justice, the rights of the lowly and the destitute.
They have refused to rescue the weak and the needy, they have not delivered them from the hand of the wicked.
And so, tho—verses 2, 3, 4, and 5 would be the case made against the gods of the nations for allowing the Judahites to be carted off into exile.
Now, normally in a psalm of complaint, you would end with your serial imperatives, and then you would move on.
That's either the end of the psalm or you would start a new—a new segment.

Because the whole point is to try to compel God to respond, to act. But obviously the gods of the nations are not going to act. The point here isn't to compel action on the part of the gods of the nations, it's to rhetorically condemn them.
And so instead of giving them an opportunity, we move back to the divine council scene, and you get the judgment against them. They have not responded,
and here is where they are consigned to mortality. You are gods, children of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, you shall die like mortals, and fall like any prince.
Now "children of the Most High" is likely a reference or an allusion to Deuteronomy 32:8 and 9,

which originally did not refer to Elyon distributing the nations according to the sons of Israel, but according to the number of the sons of God. בני אלהים is the reading preserved in 4QDeuteronomy-j at Qumran,
and is clearly the source text for the translation in the Septuagint.
So this is likely an allusion to that, as well as to this worldview that held that every nation had a sovereign patron deity over it.
Deuteronomy 32:8 and 9 suggest that, distributing the nations according to the number of the sons of God,
and יהוה's heritage or inheritance was Israel, Jacob, the lot of his inheritance.
And this is reflected in a number of preexilic texts where this worldview is maintained, that יהוה's sovereignty extends to the borders of Israel and no further.
For instance, when Naaman comes and is healed, he says, "There is no god in all the earth except inside Israel."
And then the next thing he does is takes two cartloads of Israelite soil back to Syria with him so he can worship יהוה,
because יהוה's sovereignty stops at the borders of Israel, so he's gonna take a chunk of Israel with him,
so that he can worship יהוה. And this is not just a foreigner's perspective.
We have the same thing with David. When Saul is pursuing David, chasing him, he's next to the borders of Israel.
He's about to be pushed outside of Israel and he says to Saul, you are chasing me out of יהוה's inheritance.
You are forcing me to worship other gods, because יהוה cannot be worshipped outside of יהוה's inheritance, which is Israel.
And we have the—this is similarly reflected in the exilic psalm that complains, How can we sing the songs of יהוה in a foreign land?
We don't have access to our deity because we are in a region where another deity is sovereign.
And so Psalm 82, in this sense, may be trying to remedy this.
So by consigning the deities of the divine council to mortality,
יהוה is also deposing them. You're no longer part of the divine council if you're no longer a deity.
And that is why the last verse returns to the psalmist, who says קומה אלהים,
just like they did in Psalm 74, but now it's not rise up and plead your case. You have just pleaded your case.
Rise up. Judge the earth, for you will inherit all nations, or you will take possession of all nations.
So the gods of the nations have been condemned to mortality, have been deposed, and now these seats sit empty.
Rise up יהוה, God, you take over direct rule of all the nation, and in that way,
יהוה's sovereignty is expanded to all the earth. Which is why the very next psalm ends by saying, you, יהוה, are Most High over all the earth.
So this is the universalization of יהוה, this is the point at which that limited sovereignty that stopped at the borders of Israel
is blown apart, and now your sovereignty covers all the earth, because the gods of the nations have been deposed
and condemned to mortality. That's a pretty significant paradigm shift. And that likely dates it to the late-exilic period or the post-exilic period.
So, some folks, some scholars—and for a long time I was one of them—thought that this was one of the earliest passages in the Hebrew Bible, on a par with Deuteronomy 32:8 and 9,
and may have even preserved this early distinction between יהוה and אל or עליון.
But I don't think that's accurate. I think this reflects an exilic or a post-exilic attempt to universalize יהוה's rule,
יהוה's sovereignty, and in—to do that, they took the divine council type-scene
and the psalm of complaint and merged them together and put a gods-complaint into the mouth of יהוה to direct at the gods of the nations so that they could be condemned and deposed.
So that's what I suggest Psalm 82 was originally written to accomplish, the universalization of יהוה within the Psalms of Asaph.
Now, we've got a much different reading in John 10. I wanna go to that real quick.
John 10:30, Jesus says "The Father and I are one." And Jesus' critics then try to stone Jesus and he asks why.
They say, "It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you, but for blasphemy, because you,
though only a human being, are making yourself God. Now, I would suggest that the lack of a definite article here means this should be understood qualitatively: you are making yourself a god.
This also makes sense of Jesus' point about what's written in the law.
So then Jesus answers, "Is it not written in your law, 'I said, you are gods'? If those to whom the word of God came
were called 'gods'—and the scripture cannot be annulled—can you say that the one whom the Father has sanctified and sent in to the world is blaspheming because I said, 'I am God's Son'?"
So how do we make sense of this? Well, there seems to be the suggestion in verse 35 that this reading, whatever reading Jesus is promoting,
is something that others already understood. There was no need to spell out exactly how he's interpreting it.
"If those to whom the word of God came were called 'gods'." So, the figures in Psalm 82 were those to whom the word of God came. So what is this a reference to?
There are a couple different readings of Psalm 82 that we know from the later rabbinic literature,
but the one that is the closest, chronologically, and the one that makes the most sense of this,
would be a reading that we find in some third- and fourth-century rabbinic texts, that interprets Psalm 82 in light of Sinai,
that Psalm 82 is a reference to the Israelites. Upon the reception of the law they are freed from the power of death.
They are rendered immortal. Basically, they are gods. But then they sin with the golden calf.
"I said, 'You are gods,' but you will die like men." In other words, you're being reconsigned to mortality
because of the sin with the golden calf. So that reading is known, and it is certainly plausible,
even probable that that reading was in circulation in the late first century CE when John was most likely written.
So I would suggest that that is our best interpretive lens for looking at what Jesus is saying.
So "if those to whom the word of God came were called gods." In other words, if the Israelites at Sinai to whom the—God's law, the word of God, came,
"can you say the one whom the Father has sanctified and sent into the world is blaspheming by saying I am God's son?"
The rhetorical force of this reading is basically saying, "The word of God rendered Israelites gods.
I am the Word of God. I have been sanctified. I have been sent into the world." Logos theology is at the root of the gospel of John.
"So how can you say that I am blaspheming by saying 'I am the Son of God,' when I am what made the Israelites gods according to your own scriptures?"
And so, it is that reception of the word that rendered them gods, and we also have this idea reflected in John 1 verse 12,
where he gave them power to become the children of God. Through what? Through the reception of the λογος, the word.
So, I think that's likely what's going on in John 10. Now that's a much different reading from Psalm 82, and why is there so much difference?
Because between the composition of Psalm 82 and the composition of John 10, we have the Greco-Roman Period,
and a lot of things changed in the Greco-Roman Period. There was a lot of literary exploration of the heavens and of who else inhabited them.
And so with the shoving down of the gods of the nations, and this reduction of the pantheon around יהוה, the gods of the nations didn't just disappear,
they turned into something else. They turned into angels. This is what we have in 1 Enoch.
This is what we have in the translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, the Septuagint.
Most of the places where בני אלהים or אלהים in reference to other gods occurs, they are reinterpreted as angels.
This is Genesis 6, Job 1 and 2 and 38:7, Deuteronomy 32:8 and 9, Deuteronomy 32:43, and a handful of other places.
The reference in Psalms *8*, "I have made you a little lower than the gods, than אלהים" gets changed to angels as well.
So this was the earliest rereading of the children of God and the gods. They're now angels.
And because of this view that there was a god over every nation, this is where we get the idea of guardian angels over nations.
So in Daniel, when it references Michael as the chief prince, the prince of Persia, the prince of Greece,
this is the Greco-Roman Period reflection of the notion of the patron deity over every nation,
only now it's just a guardian angel over every nation.
Now this reading caused issues of its own, because in Genesis 6—if we read Genesis 6, which talks about the children of God
having offspring with the daughters of humanity—if we read that as a reference to angels it raises two complications
for some streams of orthodoxy in this period. One, angels were sexually compatible with human women?
Two, angels could be disobedient? Now these two things caused some problems for some, and so different readings arose,
and there's a great paper by Philip Alexander on some of the early reinterpretations of Genesis 6.
But some folks wanted to move away from the angelic reading. And so they came up with a human reading.
And this is where we get the notion of—the Sethian approach to Genesis 6. That these children of God were the line of Seth.
And so that is—and we see both, kind of dimply reflected in the New Testament,
with both references to both angels and humans. But by the time of the first century, the human reading of Genesis 6
seems to have influenced the reinterpretation of Psalm 82, not as a reference to angels, who could not be disobedient anyway,
but as a reference to humans. And the gravitational pull of Sinai within Israel's or Judah's sacred past
seems to have moved the reading towards understanding it as a reference to Sinai.
And so, that is why we have a much different reading of Psalm 82 in John 10.
And, yeah, it's a fascinating psalm. When we try to treat them univocally—to say Jesus' reading has to be right,
therefore, Psalm 82 on its own, in its original contexts, must be read to agree with Jesus' reading, that's just dogmatism.
We need to let these texts operate on their own terms, and that meant different contexts, different rhetorical goals,
different authors, different audiences. And so, I suggest we need to let these two texts operate as very very different texts in those two different contexts,
Psalm 82 within the Psalms of Asaph within the book of Psalms, and then this quote within John 10.
So, I will link in the description of the video to my paper from the Journal of Biblical Literature on Psalm 82.
I also published a paper a couple years earlier on Psalm 82 in the Latter-day Saint tradition,
where I talk about how Latter-day Saints tend to read Psalm 82, and it's primarily through the lens of John 10,
and we tend to use it as a proof text for this notion that humans are the offspring of deity.
And so, "you are children of God," or "you are gods, children of the Most High."
That's something that we actually, we reference Psalm 82:6 in some of our literature for Primary children,
which I have long said is not a great idea. But I'll link to that paper as well, cuz that goes into more detail
about how I suggest we read Psalm 82 through John 10. But, yeah, those are my thoughts on Psalm 82. I hope you'll let me know if there's anything else you'd like me to address,
if there—you have any lingering questions about Psalm 82 or its use in John 10 that you would like me to address.
I appreciate it. Hope y'all are having a great day.
